title: Brushing my teeth
keyIdea: Brush your teeth twice a day: last thing at night and one other time. Brush for about 2 minutes, gently, in small circles. Clean every tooth on the outside, the inside and the chewing tops, and along the gums. Use a pea-sized blob of fluoride toothpaste. Spit it out, but do not rinse with water, so the fluoride stays on your teeth. Keep sweet food and drinks to mealtimes, because each sugary snack starts an acid attack on teeth that lasts up to an hour.
familyTip: Brush together tonight with an egg timer or a 2-minute song. Let your child brush first, then you finish off and check the insides and the tops. Squeeze the pea-sized blob together, and make 'spit, don't rinse' the last step before bed, with only water after it.

visual.caption: Good for teeth or not? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: scrub plaque off every side, squeeze a pea and a smear, brush four parts for 2 minutes, put bedtime brushing in order, move treats to mealtimes.

kid: Sticky plaque grows on your teeth every day. It is made of germs. Brushing takes it off. Brush the outside, the inside next to your tongue, and the tops you chew with. The front is only one side.

Use a blob of toothpaste the size of a pea. More does not clean better, and a baby needs only a tiny smear. Brush gently in small circles for about 2 minutes, so every part of your mouth gets a turn: top and bottom, this side and that side.
When you finish, spit the toothpaste out. Do not rinse with water. The toothpaste has fluoride in it, and fluoride keeps your teeth strong if you leave it there.

Sweet things make acid in your mouth. Each time you eat or drink something sweet, the acid works on your teeth for up to an hour. So have sweet things with meals, not a bit all day. After the bedtime brush, only water.
adult: Ages 4 to 5. This follows NHS advice for children aged 3 to 6. Brush at least twice a day for about 2 minutes: last thing at night and one other time. Use a pea-sized blob of fluoride toothpaste (1,000 to 1,500 ppm fluoride). Then spit it out and do not rinse, because rinsing washes the fluoride away. Children under 3 need only a smear. Let your child brush, and watch and help. The NHS says most children can brush on their own from about 7. Key words: plaque, fluoride, toothpaste, gums, spit, rinse.

Plaque is a sticky layer of germs. When we eat or drink something sugary, the germs turn the sugar into acid. Teeth are then under acid attack for up to about an hour (Oral Health Foundation; NHS dental diet leaflets). So how often matters, not just how much. Three sweets eaten with lunch make one attack. The same sweets nibbled all afternoon make several. That is why sweet food and drinks are best kept to mealtimes, with water or milk in between. After the bedtime brush, only water.

Common mistakes: brushing only the front teeth, a long stripe of toothpaste, a quick ten-second brush, scrubbing hard, rinsing straight after brushing, and juice or milk after the bedtime brush. Be careful not to scare your child about holes in teeth. The aim is a calm routine you do together every night.

In the lab your child scrubs plaque off the outside, inside and tops of four teeth. They squeeze a pea-sized blob for themselves and a smear for a baby. They brush four parts of the mouth until a timer reaches 2 minutes. They put bedtime brushing in order and see rinsing wash the fluoride off. Last, they move juice, sweets and a biscuit to mealtimes, which cuts the acid attacks from 6 to 3. In the lab, each meal counts as one attack, a simple model of the real thing.

practice.prompt: Which parts of each tooth do you brush?
choices: The outside, the inside and the top
Only the teeth at the back
practice.hint: Think about the side next to your tongue, and the part you chew with.
practice.explain: Brush every side: the outside, the inside next to your tongue, and the chewing tops. Plaque hides on all of them.

practice.prompt: You brush your teeth 2 times every day. How many times is that in {a} days?
practice.hint: Count in twos: 2 for each day. Add 2 for every day.
practice.explain: 2 times a day for {a} days makes {=2*a} brushes: one at bedtime and one other time, every day.

practice.prompt: {a} teeth have plaque on the outside and {b} teeth have plaque on the inside. How many places do you need to brush?
practice.hint: Count the outsides, then count on the insides.
practice.explain: {a} outsides and {b} insides make {=a+b} places to brush. The inside counts just as much as the outside.

practice.prompt: You have finished brushing. What do you do next?
choices: Spit it out, and do not rinse
practice.hint: The fluoride works best if it stays on your teeth.
practice.explain: Spit the toothpaste out but do not rinse, so the fluoride stays on your teeth. After the bedtime brush, only water.

practice.prompt: How much toothpaste do you put on your brush?
choices: A blob the size of a pea
practice.hint: More toothpaste does not clean better.
practice.explain: A pea-sized blob is right for children aged 3 to 6. A baby under 3 needs only a tiny smear.

pool.prompt: How long do you brush your teeth?
pool.hint: Every part of your mouth needs a turn.
pool.explain: About 2 minutes, so the top and bottom, this side and that side all get brushed. A quick brush misses plaque.

pool.prompt: When is the best time for a sweet treat?
pool.hint: Each sweet snack starts a new acid attack.
pool.explain: With a meal. Teeth are already having one acid attack at the meal, so the treat does not start a new one.

pool.prompt: When do you brush your teeth?
choices: Last thing at night and one other time
pool.hint: Twice a day, and one of those is at bedtime.
pool.explain: Twice a day: last thing at night and one other time, such as in the morning.

pool.prompt: You eat 3 meals. You also have {a} sweet snacks between meals. Each meal and each sweet snack makes an acid attack. How many acid attacks is that?
pool.hint: Start at 3 for the meals, then count on 1 for each sweet snack.
pool.explain: 3 meals and {a} sweet snacks make {=3+a} acid attacks. Moving the sweets to mealtimes would make it just 3.

pool.prompt: Why do you not rinse after brushing?
pool.hint: Think about what is in the toothpaste.
pool.explain: Toothpaste has fluoride, which keeps teeth strong. Rinsing washes it away, so just spit.

pool.hint: Think about your soft gums, and what hard scrubbing would do to them.
pool.explain: Gently, in small circles, along the gums too. Scrubbing hard can hurt your gums and does not clean better.

pool.prompt: You brush the outside of {a} teeth. Then you brush the inside of the same {a} teeth. How many sides did you brush?
pool.hint: Add the outsides and the insides: the same number twice.
pool.explain: {a} outsides and {a} insides make {=a+a} sides. Do not forget the chewing tops too!

pool.prompt: How much toothpaste does a baby under 3 need?
pool.explain: A tiny smear for a baby under 3. A pea-sized blob for children aged 3 to 6.
